W7222540514.abstract: The transition from fossil-based plastics to bioplastics in food packaging requires not only technological advances but also coherent regulatory frameworks and economic support mechanisms. This review examines how policies, production costs, and industrial initiatives shape the large-scale adoption of biopolymers such as polylactic acid (PLA), polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA), and starch-based materials. The regulatory comparison indicates substantial differences in legal scope and implementation across jurisdictions, while also showing that the existence of binding legislation does not by itself demonstrate bioplastic-specific circular-performance outcomes. Although the high production cost of bioplastics remains a major barrier to widespread implementation, strategies including agricultural residue valorization and green fiscal instruments may contribute to improving competitiveness. Overall, the evidence reviewed suggests that the transition toward sustainable food packaging depends on the combined development of material performance, regulatory coherence, industrial integration, and life-cycle accountability, highlighting the need for greater coordination across these dimensions.
W7222540514.title: Bioplastics Beyond Materials: A Review on Regulatory, Economic, and Circular Pathways Toward Sustainable Food Packaging

W7222541572.abstract: The disposal of tannery effluent containing trivalent chromium (Cr(III)) is a major environmental concern. This study focuses on the preparation, characterization, and Cr(III) adsorption capacity of biochar from Spondias mombin ( S. mombin ) seed. The dried S. mombin seeds were thermally activated at 400±5°C for 150 min in a furnace. The comprehensive characterization of biochar was conducted using FTIR, SEM, EDS, XRD, BET, and pHpzc. Batch adsorption achieved about 99.98% Cr(III) removal under optimal conditions: a biochar dose of 0.4 g/50 mL, 20 min of stirring, 30 min of settling, and 30°C, with a solution pH of 6.9. The adsorption primarily occurred on the positively charged surface of biochar, which had a specific surface area of 5.922 m 2 /g, and then precipitation occurred at that pH. The adsorption of Cr(III) on biochar followed the Freundlich adsorption isotherm (R 2 = 0.9772) and the Pseudo-Second-Order kinetic model, with high correlation coefficients. Thus, the derived biochar from S. mombin seeds represents a viable option for mitigating Cr(III) in tannery effluent prior to disposal. The efficient adsorption capacity of biochar derived from waste materials is a step towards sustainable waste management across industries, in line with green development goals.

W7222541841.abstract: High-performance textiles demand fibre architectures that combine mechanical integrity, efficient moisture transport for wearer comfort, and scalable processing, all while meeting stringent sustainability expectations in one of the world’s most environmentally burdensome industries. Here we present a proof of concept for engineering capillary moisture transport into polyethylene by melt-spinning bicomponent fibres with a high-density polyethylene (HDPE) core and polylactic acid (PLA) shell that was selectively dissolved after weaving. Fibres collected at winding speeds of 1000 and 2000 metres per minute (mpm) exhibited mean diameters of 11.96 ± 0.85 μm and 9.63 ± 0.94 μm, respectively, and HDPE crystallinities of 65.6% and 68.7% by DSC. TGA showed that PLA degraded first, with an onset at 293 °C, compared with 395 °C for the fibres recovered after dissolution (HDPEAD). After selective PLA removal, SEM revealed aligned inter-fibre channels and longitudinal surface ridges consistent with along-the-fibre water transport, and infra-red thermography showed that the resulting woven HDPEAD fabrics wick water, reaching saturation in 7-8 min (n = 3), compared with 4 min for cotton and 2 min for polyester, whereas TyvekTM (a commercial nonwoven of flash-spun HDPE) showed no uptake under the same conditions.
W7222541841.title: Melt-spun HDPE/PLA core–shell fibres: a sacrificial-shell route to capillary moisture transport in polyethylene textiles

W7222572719.abstract: How homologous straw and biochar alter soil carbon fractions and associated microbial processes in coastal saline soils remains unclear. A 120-day microcosm experiment compared reed (Phragmites australis) straw and its biochar at equal mass rates of 1%, 5%, and 9% of dry soil mass. Both amendments increased the soil organic carbon (SOC) and reduced electrical conductivity. At 9%, straw increased the particulate organic carbon share of SOC to 78.2%, decreased the bacterial oligotroph/copiotroph ratio from 1.82 to 0.86, and raised potential hydrolytic enzyme activities to 4.3–9.1 times the control levels. Across straw treatments, cumulative CO2 emissions were 375.0–1645.9% higher than in the unamended control. Biochar maintained operationally defined mineral-associated organic carbon dominance (62.1–68.0% of SOC), with weaker hydrolytic responses and cumulative CO2 emissions 58.0–102.2% above the control levels. Exploratory structural equation models showed that lower bacterial oligotroph/copiotroph ratios were associated with higher hydrolytic enzyme activity under straw. Under biochar, higher fungal Basidiomycota/Ascomycota ratios were associated with higher polyphenol oxidase activity. Both enzyme indicators were positively associated with cumulative CO2 emissions in their respective models. These findings demonstrate contrasting carbon fraction distributions and respiratory responses to homologous amendments, with implications for carbon management in coastal saline soils.
W7222572719.title: Divergent Impacts of Straw and Biochar on Organic Carbon Fraction Allocation and CO2 Emissions in Coastal Saline Soil

W7222600295.abstract: Abstract Fused filament fabrication (FFF) produces strong, direction-dependent elastic anisotropy that conventional uniaxial testing cannot fully capture. This study introduces a multiaxial ultrasonic methodology that identifies the complete orthotropic stiffness tensor of FFF-printed polylactic acid (PLA) and PLA/wood-flour (PLA/WF) composites and uses it to quantify how layer thickness, infill density and infill pattern control their directional elastic response. Chamfered cubic specimens (72 in total, 24 processing configurations, three replicates each) were tested along three principal axes and three face-diagonal directions to obtain the nine independent stiffness coefficients, with a within-configuration repeatability of 1.2–6.2 %. Infill pattern is the principal driver of elastic anisotropy: the in-plane stiffness ratio E2/E1 reaches 2.9 for the Line pattern at low infill density, against near-unity values for the Combined pattern. Wood flour redistributes stiffness preferentially transverse to the filaments at low infill density, recovering E₁ by up to 110 % and reducing in-plane anisotropy by up to 41 %, while the build direction remains intrinsically softer than the in-plane directions regardless of raster orientation. Compliance-matrix inversion further suggests apparent near-zero or negative Poisson’s ratios (ν₁₂ as low as −0.06) for one Line-pattern configuration at low infill density; this auxetic-like response is reported as a working hypothesis requiring direct strain-field validation. A four-way ANOVA on the raw replicate measurements confirms these trends quantitatively, with highly significant effects of infill density and material on all nine stiffness coefficients (p < 0.0001) and significant material × density interactions for eight of the nine coefficients (p < 0.05). Acoustic microscopy supports these findings by revealing inter-raster voiding, wood-flour-mediated bridging and layer-thickness-dependent interlayer features. The proposed framework offers a non-destructive route to the complete elastic characterization of FFF-printed biobased composites and quantitative guidance for the design of structurally anisotropic components.
W7222600295.title: Process-microstructure-anisotropy relationships in FFF-printed PLA/wood flour composites: Multiaxial ultrasonic determination of the orthotropic elastic tensor

W7222629347.abstract: Earlier sludge-focused reviews mapped the occurrence and detection of microplastics (MPs) in sewage sludge. This mini-review addresses a subsequent gap: the 2025–2026 evidence on dual particle- versus mass-based inventories, the interaction of MPs with antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) under aging and polymer type, thermal hydrolysis process (THP) control of those markers, and laboratory- to pilot-scale adsorbents and process trains. Sewage sludge is a major sink for MPs that enter wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs). Conventional wastewater treatment moves a large share of MPs to the solid residuals, while specialized industrial streams can bring higher loads. Risk is thereby redistributed toward sludge rather than eliminated. National assessments confirm that sludge is essential for the terrestrial spread of MPs. Sludge processing stimulates interactions between MPs and the biological and thermal steps: composting or digestion can enrich or shift ARGs and mobile genetic elements; THP suppresses these markers. Sequential thermal–biological trains achieve the lowest final MP abundances reported among the compared configurations. Aged MPs enhance conjugative gene transfer. MP-derived dissolved organic matter (DOM) adds to the soluble carbon pool. Certain polyethylene particles affect methane generation in size-dependent ways. MPs also raise ARG abundance in sludge, intestinal, and plant settings. Biodegradable polymers may cause more severe adverse effects on resistance and virulence profiles than conventional plastics. Biochar amendments either accelerate MP degradation or provide high adsorption capacity for MPs. Advanced mass-based methods improve quantification accuracy. Integrated thermal–biological trains and engineered adsorbents currently offer the most promising control routes, although full-scale validation remains limited. The challenges and research and development needs for handling MPs in wastewater sludge are outlined at the end of this mini-review.
W7222629347.title: Microplastics in Wastewater Treatment Plants and Sewage Sludge: Occurrence, Fate under Treatment, Impacts, and Mitigation

W7222631494.title: A review on industrial wastewater pollution: key contaminants and advanced treatment technologies

W7222631773.abstract: The growing accumulation of Pinus roxburghii needles in the Indian Himalayan region presents both a significant fire hazard and an underutilized biomass resource. This study investigates the conversion of pine needles into bio-oil and biochar through bench-scale pyrolysis, with process optimization using Response Surface Methodology (RSM). In contrast to previous studies largely limited to laboratory-scale investigations, this work demonstrates the scale-up potential of pine needle pyrolysis and provides data relevant to its practical deployment. Product characterization confirmed the successful conversion of pine needles into value-added products, with biochar exhibiting enhanced carbon-rich properties and bio-oil containing diverse organic compounds. The findings not only validate RSM as a robust optimization tool for scale-up but also highlight the potential of pine needle pyrolysis products for renewable energy, carbon sequestration and environmental applications. By converting a fire-prone forest residue into valuable bioenergy products, this study contributes to sustainable biomass valorization and forest fire risk mitigation.
W7222631773.title: Pyrolysis of Pinus roxburghii: process optimization, product characterization and scale-up potential

W7222638148.abstract: Abstract This study quantifies the gross ecosystem-service benefits of biochar-mediated soil erosion control across climate, agricultural, and water-system pathways, while treating runoff reduction as a non-monetised hydrological co-benefit. Soil erosion is a major driver of land degradation, with global losses exceeding billions of tonnes annually and affecting approximately 24% of European land. Meta-analytical evidence indicates that biochar application reduces soil erosion by 16% and surface runoff by 25% on average, with stronger effects observed in erosion-prone environments. Using this evidence, three baseline erosion scenarios were evaluated. Under low, moderate, and high baseline erosion scenarios, central gross benefits were €2.80, €9.33, and €24.19 ha⁻ 1 yr⁻ 1 , respectively. Monte Carlo analysis yielded median total values of €2.95 (95% uncertainty interval: €1.36–€7.48), €9.85 (€4.54–€24.92), and €25.52 (€13.81–€56.21) ha⁻ 1 yr⁻ 1 , respectively. These estimates exclude biochar production, transport, and application costs and therefore represent gross co-benefits rather than net economic returns. Mediterranean experiments reported erosion reductions of up to 67%, substantially above the global mean, illustrating the strong context dependence of biochar responses but not providing a basis for regional economic extrapolation. The results identify soil erosion control as a potentially measurable co-benefit of biochar deployment across climate, agricultural, and water systems. The framework provides a transparent basis for future site- and region-specific valuation while explicitly accounting for uncertainty in biophysical and economic parameters.
W7222638148.title: A scenario-based economic valuation framework for ecosystem service benefits of biochar-mediated soil erosion control

W7222645082.abstract: Decarbonising road materials requires scalable strategies that enhance durability while valorising waste streams. This study investigates the effect of antioxidant biochar derived from European hazelnut shells (BH) on the operational and rheological performance of a PG 64–22 asphalt binder. BH was produced via slow pyrolysis at 300 °C and incorporated at contents of 2.5, 5.0 and 7.5 wt% using two particle size fractions (S < 20 μm and L < 75 μm). Owing to its carbon-rich composition and the presence of antioxidant compounds reported in previous studies, BH was evaluated as a sustainable modifier with the potential to improve the ageing resistance of asphalt binders. Commercial graphite was included as a control modifier for comparison. Operational properties were assessed through rotational viscosity and storage stability, while rheological performance was evaluated using the rutting parameter G*/sin(δ), Bending Beam Rheometer (BBR), Multiple Stress Creep and Recovery (MSCR), |G*| and δ master curves, rheological ageing index (RAI), and time sweep fatigue tests. BH increased rotational viscosity and mixing and compaction temperatures without compromising storage stability. At high temperatures, BH enhanced rutting resistance by increasing G*/sin(δ) and reducing the non-recoverable creep compliance ( Jnr ), particularly for the finer particle size fraction. At low temperatures, BH increased creep stiffness without significantly affecting the stress relaxation capacity compared with control binders. Master curve and RAI analysis indicated lower susceptibility to long-term ageing-induced stiffening at higher BH contents. BH also improved the fatigue response by increasing accumulated dissipated energy and tended to delay the 50% reduction of the initial |G*| compared with the unmodified binder. Based on the combined rheological response, 5.0 wt% BH with a particle size below 20 μm was selected as the final formulation for this type of modifier.
W7222645082.title: Balanced asphalt binder performance with hazelnut shell biochar

W7222645182.title: Mixed-Carbon Fermentation with Hydrocarbons and Fatty Acids for Enhanced Medium-Chain-Length Polyhydroxyalkanoate Production

W7222653583.abstract: : Poly(lactic acid)/poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PLA/PBAT) and poly(lactic acid)/poly(butylene succinate) (PLA/PBS) biodegradable polymer blends were prepared with weight ratios of 100/0, 75/25, 50/50, 25/75, and 0/100 to investigate how blend composition and phase morphology affect dynamic energy absorption. Rheological properties, phase morphology, and impact behavior were characterized for solid materials before foaming. Asymmetric blend ratios showed typical sea-island morphologies, whereas at 50/50 weight ratio, the PLA/PBAT blends formed a strongly interconnected, co-continuous structure, while PLA/PBS showed elongated and fibrillar domains with a lower degree of interconnection. Rheological analysis showed viscosity ratios close to unity for PLA/PBAT and a substantially larger viscosity mismatch for PLA/PBS, consistent with the observed morphologies. Neat PLA showed a thickness-normalized perforation energy of approximately 0.2-0.4 J/mm, whereas at a 50/50 blend ratio it increased to 2.67 J/mm for PLA/PBS and 10.18-10.73 J/mm for PLA/PBAT, depending on the PLA grade. In both blend systems, the energy absorption of the 50/50 composition also outperformed the corresponding neat secondary polymer. The blends were then foamed by flat-sheet extrusion using 2, 4, and 8 wt% thermally expandable microspheres. The foamed samples were evaluated by density measurements, cellular morphology analysis, and falling weight impact tests. Increasing microsphere content reduced relative density to approximately 0.38-0.55 at 8 wt%, corresponding to a density reduction of 45-62%, while the effect of blend composition on density remained secondary. At higher microsphere contents, the influence of the original phase morphology on impact behavior became less pronounced and the cellular structure increasingly influenced the perforation response.
W7222653583.journal: Advanced Industrial and Engineering Polymer Research
W7222653583.title: Energy Absorption of PLA/PBAT and PLA/PBS Biodegradable Polymer Blends: Phase Morphology and Microsphere-Based Foaming

W7222660579.abstract: The effects of biochar on soil fertility and maize yield were investigated in controlled experiments.The impact of different biochar treatments on plant growth, growth physiology and yield was evaluated using a randomized multiple replication design.Throughout the growth period, key growth indicators such as plant height, biomass growth, chlorophyll content and photosynthetic activity were measured.In addition, soil nutrient availability, water use efficiency and yield components were assessed to assess the overall impact of biochar on soil-plant interaction.The biochar resulted in a significant increase in soil fertility and maize performance, relative to the control.Physiological responses were stronger due to the improved soil nutrient retention, increased soil moisture availability, and increased microbial activity.The results showed that these changes were manifested in the form of an increase in photosynthetic efficiency, the amount of chlorophyll and biomass production.In conclusion, maize planted under biochar amendment yielded better in terms of higher production and resource use efficiency.Biochar treatments found to have significant impacts through statistical analysis on most of the growth, physiological and yield parameters.In general, biochar has excellent potential as a soil amendment to enhance the productivity of maize while maintaining the sustainability of agricultural production and management, and to facilitate sustainable nutrient use.
W7222660579.title: Effects of Biochar Application on Soil Fertility and Maize Productivity

W7222668908.abstract: Most tropical soils exhibit low phosphorus (P) availability and a high adsorption capacity, resulting in low recovery of fertilizer-applied P. In addition to soil mineralogy, contact time, fertilizer source, and the type of coating (technology) employed also influence P availability in the soil. In this context, the development of fertilizers incorporating new technologies has been proposed to increase the efficiency of phosphate fertilization. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of different technologies associated with MAP on soil phosphorus availability, assessed by water-extractable P (P-H2O) and Mehlich-1-extractable P (P-M1), and on maize development, assessed by shoot dry matter production (SDMP) and leaf area (LA), after soil pre-incubation with the fertilizers for periods of up to 150 days. The treatments consisted of conventional monoammonium phosphate (MAP), polymer-coated MAP (MAPPOL), MAP combined with sugarcane filter cake (MAPFC), and MAP combined with coffee-husk biochar (MAPBIO). Treatments were arranged in a split-plot design with four replications, where the main plot consisted of four phosphate fertilizers MAP, MAPPOL, MAPFC, and MAPBIO, and the subplot consisted of incubation periods (15, 30, 60, 90, 120, and 150 days). Two successive cultivation cycles, each lasting 30 days, were conducted. Collectively, the three slow-release fertilizers evaluated—polymer-coated MAP (MAPPOL), MAP combined with filter cake (MAPFC), and biochar-coated MAP (MAPBIO)—resulted in higher mean P-H2O than conventional MAP (31.48 versus 26.10 mg dm−3, respectively). These fertilizers also resulted in higher P-M1 mean values than conventional MAP (273.04 and 194.44 mg dm−3, respectively). The coated fertilizers (MAPPOL and MAPBIO) generally promoted higher P-H2O and P-M1 values than the fertilizer containing the organic additive (MAPFC) throughout the 150-day incubation period. MAPBIO exhibited higher P-H2O and P-M1 values than MAPPOL during the evaluated period. In the first cultivation cycle, MAP produced better results than the slow-release fertilizers for SDMP-1 and LA-1, with average values of 14.59 g and 4061.28 cm2 for MAP and 14.12 g and 3513.63 cm2 for the slow-release fertilizers, respectively. In the second 30-day cultivation cycle, however, slow-release fertilizers outperformed MAP, with average values of 13.17 g and 3590.29 cm2 for the slow-release fertilizers and 11.83 g and 3282.22 cm2 for MAP, respectively. For both variables, MAPPOL and MAPBIO performed better than MAPFC.
W7222668908.title: Phosphorus Availability in Soils Previously Fertilized with Slow-Release Phosphate Fertilizers

W7222695559.title: Optimized production of polyhydroxyalkanoates from Priestia megaterium using sugar beet molasses: a cost-effective approach for eco-friendly bioplastics

W7222699158.abstract: Oral drug delivery remains the most widely preferred route of drug administration owing to its convenience, patient compliance, cost-effectiveness, and suitability for long-term therapy.However, the oral delivery of many therapeutic agents is significantly limited by poor aqueous solubility, low intestinal permeability, gastrointestinal degradation, extensive first-pass metabolism, and efflux transporter activity, resulting in inadequate bioavailability and inconsistent therapeutic outcomes.Polymeric nanospheres have emerged as a promising nanotechnology-based platform capable of overcoming these physiological and biopharmaceutical barriers through enhanced drug protection, controlled release, improved mucosal interaction, and targeted intestinal absorption.The selection of appropriate biodegradable polymers, together with advances in formulation technologies such as nanoprecipitation, solvent evaporation, microfluidics, and continuous manufacturing, has considerably improved the physicochemical properties and therapeutic performance of oral nanosphere formulations.Furthermore, recent developments in surface engineering, stimuli-responsive polymers, artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted formulation design, machine learning (ML), and Quality by Design (QbD) have accelerated the optimization and translation of polymeric nanospheres from laboratory research toward industrial manufacturing.This review comprehensively summarizes the fundamental principles, classification, formulation strategies, characterization techniques, drug release mechanisms, surface functionalization approaches, and smart polymeric nanosphere systems developed for oral drug delivery.In addition, recent therapeutic applications in cancer, diabetes, infectious diseases, inflammatory disorders, neurological diseases, and biological therapeutics are critically discussed.The review also highlights current translational challenges, regulatory considerations, clinical perspectives, and future research directions with particular emphasis on intelligent nanomedicine, precision drug delivery, and sustainable pharmaceutical manufacturing.Overall, polymeric nanospheres represent a versatile and rapidly evolving oral drug delivery platform with significant potential to improve drug bioavailability, therapeutic efficacy, and patient outcomes while facilitating the development of next-generation oral nanomedicines.
W7222699158.journal: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
W7222699158.title: POLYMERIC NANOSPHERES FOR ORAL DRUG DELIVERY: EMERGING FORMULATION TECHNOLOGIES, TRANSLATIONAL CHALLENGES, AND FUTURE CLINICAL PERSPECTIVES

W7222717997.abstract: Abstract Purpose The successful establishment of perennial species in agroforestry systems depends critically on nursery-phase conditions, yet evidence on alternative growing media remains fragmented across species, crop groups, and experimental contexts. This study synthesized evidence on peat-reduced and alternative nursery substrates to identify recurrent substrate systems and physicochemical conditions associated with high performance in tropical perennial seedlings relevant to agroforestry. Methods We conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review and quantitative synthesis integrating treatment-level Composite Performance Index (CPI) values, physicochemical modelling, empirical quality-control windows, and a supplementary log response ratio (lnRR) meta-analytic layer. The deduplicated evidence base comprised 84 eligible studies distributed across the tropical belt. Results Coir/cocopeat-based mixes showed the strongest recurrent integrated-performance signal, with the highest median CPI (0.569) and the greatest proportion of treatments above the 70th percentile threshold (51.3%). Vermicompost-based mixes, agroindustrial residues, and selected biochar-amended media also performed well. Bulk density showed the strongest negative association with CPI (standardized β = −0.339), whereas nitrogen, total organic carbon, cation exchange capacity, and phosphorus were positively associated with performance. pH and electrical conductivity showed nonlinear responses, with peak performance at intermediate values. Conclusions High-performing tropical nursery media were defined less by a single ingredient than by a coherent physicochemical profile. The resulting framework provides evidence-based guidance for designing regionally adapted, peat-reduced growing media for perennial planting material used in agroforestry systems.
W7222717997.journal: Journal of soil science and plant nutrition
W7222717997.title: Peat-Free Growing Media for Tropical Agroforestry Seedlings: A Systematic Review and Predictive Substrate-Quality Framework with Supplementary Multilevel Meta-Analysis

W7222720657.abstract: Aim. To determine the effects of alfalfa proportion and biostimulant application on the photosynthetic performance of perennial legume–grass swards. Methods. The study was conducted in 2021–2023 at the Agronomic Research Station of the National University of Life and Environmental Sciences of Ukraine in the Right-Bank Forest-Steppe of Ukraine. A two-factor experiment compared an alfalfa monoculture, a grass-only sward, and legume–grass mixtures containing 35–75% alfalfa under three treatments: no biostimulants, biochar application (250 kg/ha), and humus extract application (50 + 50 L/ha). Photosynthetic potential, net assimilation rate, photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) use efficiency, pigment content, and gas exchange parameters were determined. Results. Depending on the alfalfa proportion, the photosynthetic potential of perennial legume–grass swards ranged from 2.28 to 3.45 million m²·days/ha, whereas net assimilation rate showed the opposite trend, decreasing from 3.23 to 2.74 g/(m²·day) as the alfalfa proportion increased. Mixtures containing 65–75% alfalfa produced the highest dry matter yields and maximum PAR use efficiency (2.02–2.03%) through an optimal combination of high photosynthetic potential and an adequate net assimilation rate. Increasing the alfalfa proportion further to 100% resulted in light limitation in the lower canopy layers and a decline in net assimilation rate, confirming the absence of a direct relationship between this parameter and yield (r = −0.076). Photosynthetic efficiency was closely related to pigment composition (r = 0.990): total chlorophyll (a + b) content consistently increased with the alfalfa proportion, reaching a maximum of 2.35 mg/g following humus extract application. Biochar and humus extract increased pigment content and net photosynthetic rate; however, the latter shifted the competitive balance in favour of grasses, reducing overall yield in some treatments despite high photosynthetic activity in individual leaves. Conclusions. Increasing the alfalfa proportion in perennial swards from 35 to 75% increased photosynthetic potential from 2.44 to 3.29 million m²·days/ha and PAR use efficiency from 1.53 to 1.93%, while net assimilation rate decreased from 3.05 to 2.86 g/(m²·day). The optimal combination is a photosynthetic potential above 3.2 million m²·days/ha and a net assimilation rate of at least 2.85 g/(m²·day).
W7222720657.title: Photosynthetic activity of grass stands depending on the composition of the grass mixture and the application of biostimulants

W7222733071.title: Mechanical, biological, and thermal performance of fused deposition modeled PLA biocomposites reinforced with sugar-beet-derived hydroxyapatite nanofillers and Montrichardia linifera microfibers

W7222736454.abstract: Gas fermentation has emerged as a promising technology for converting C1 gaseous substrates, such as carbon monoxide (CO), carbon dioxide (CO2), and hydrogen (H2), into biofuels and platform chemicals using acetogenic microorganisms. Driven by global carbon reduction and carbon neutrality goals, this technology has attracted increasing attention due to its ability to fix carbon under mild conditions while directly utilizing industrial off-gases or renewable syngas. Consequently, it offers significant environmental and economic benefits in carbon recycling. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in gas fermentation, beginning with the key functional microorganisms involved, with particular emphasis on acetogenic bacteria and their Wood-Ljungdahl pathway. The metabolic features and energy conservation strategies of this pathway are discussed to illustrate its central role in converting C1 substrates into acetyl-CoA. Subsequently, major gaseous feedstocks—including industrial off-gases, biomass-derived syngas, and CO2/H2 mixtures—are categorized and compared in terms of their availability, composition, and application potential. The main fermentation products are then reviewed, focusing on acetate and ethanol as the most established compounds. In addition, recent studies have demonstrated the feasibility of producing a wider range of value-added chemicals through metabolic engineering and process integration, including medium-chain carboxylic acids (e.g., butyrate and caproate), their corresponding alcohols (e.g., butanol and hexanol), and biopolymers such as polyhydroxyalkanoates. Despite these advances, several key challenges still limit the large-scale application of gas fermentation, including gas–liquid mass transfer limitations resulting from the inherently low solubility of gaseous substrates, the relatively narrow product spectrum of native acetogens, and difficulties in controlling product selectivity under industrial conditions. Finally, future perspectives are proposed to address these challenges. Strategies such as reactor and process optimization are expected to enhance gas–liquid mass transfer efficiency, while adaptive laboratory evolution and metabolic engineering may expand product diversity and improve carbon conversion efficiency. Furthermore, integrating gas fermentation with downstream bioprocesses—particularly chain elongation—offers a promising route to convert primary metabolites into higher-value chemicals. Through these advances, gas fermentation is expected to play an increasingly important role in circular carbon utilization and sustainable chemical production.

W7222737766.abstract: Microplastics (MPs; < 5 mm) and Nanoplastics (NPs; 1 nm - 1 µm) are persistent contaminants in agricultural ecosystems and originate from plastic mulching, irrigation systems, packaging products, improper waste management, and atmospheric deposition. Their accumulation in soils is a concern for soil productivity, health, and safety and, by extension, food safety. The impacts of MPs and NPs on crop systems are reviewed with respect to the influence of polymer characteristics, size of the MPs and NPs, concentration of their exposure, and plant species. It also evaluates the potential for existing mitigation and remediation strategies. MPs and NPs can have an impact on seed germination, root growth, photosynthesis, nutrient assimilation, oxidation-reduction processes, and molecular responses in plants. The effects depend on the type of polymer, particle size, conditions, and concentrations. Smaller NPs tend to be more mobile and accessible to the cells, while MPs can impact plants via physical interference, soil structural modification, and microbial interactions. Additives and surface properties have a strong influence on toxicity; some polymers are more toxic than others. While these methods, such as microbial degradation, application of biochar, phytoremediation, and nanotechnology-based methods, are promising, it is hampered by cost, efficiency, and environmental restrictions when applied at a large scale. Emphasis needs to be placed on preventive systems, plastic management, and proven remediation systems. Long-term field studies, plant uptake mechanisms, toxicities of different polymer types, co-contaminant interactions, and food-chain transfer of plastics should be investigated in the future to provide sustainable solutions to plastic pollution in agriculture.
W7222737766.title: Current and Future Trends in Microplastics and Nanoplastics Alleviation from Croplands: A Threat to Agriculture, Finance, and Economy

W7222747813.abstract: Abstract Ineffective management of agricultural residues poses serious environmental challenges. In this context, the transformation of agricultural biomass into value-added products has become increasingly important. Agricultural reuse of medicinal and aromatic plant residues and their metabolites may be beneficial for being generally less harmful than conventional (synthetic) fertilizers, having reduced persistence in the environment, and limiting the development of pathogen resistance for their chemical complexity. Consequently, MAP biomasses represent promising candidates for valorisation as soil amendments. The aim of the present work was to assess the current state of knowledge on the reuse and soil application of MAP residues and to identify the plant species that have been most extensively investigated. An increasing research interest in this topic has been observed, particularly over the last five years. The families Asteraceae, Fabaceae, and Lamiaceae have emerged as those receiving the greatest scientific attention. Four main categories of MAP waste used as soil amendments were identified: fresh biomass, biochar, compost, and solid distillation residues. Overall, the reported outcomes highlight the positive effects of these materials as soil conditioners (improving soil properties, promoting crop growth and limiting weed emergence) and underline their considerable potential. Nevertheless, further research is required to find a proper balance between herbicide and biostimulant effects and optimize the use of MAP-derived residues in soil, especially at field scale.
W7222747813.title: Valorisation of medicinal and aromatic plant residues for soil amendment purposes

W7222752631.abstract: Abstract Pulp fiber-reinforced polymer nanocomposites have received considerable R&D interest, with a notable challenge in achieving good nanofiber dispersion. One particularly successful approach is through the in situ fibrillation of the pulp fibers into nanofibers in the presence of polymers during extrusion compounding. The extrusion fibrillation of bleached/unbleached pulp fibers and old corrugated container was investigated with polylactic acid (PLA) for improving fiber dispersion. Extrusion fibrillation generated both fibrillated nanofibers and unfibrillated pulp fibers, which were well dispersed in the PLA matrix. PLA’s crystallinity increased as fiber loading increased, attributable to the nucleating effect of cellulose. Heat deflection temperature increased from 53 °C to 57 °C with fiber presence at high loading. Higher fiber loading also increased the viscosity of composite melts because of increased fiber−fiber and fiber−polymer interactions. The biocomposites formed were found to have improved tensile strength (∼75 MPa) and stiffness (∼5.5 GPa) by 15% and 53%, respectively, at a 30 wt. % fiber loading relative to the neat PLA polymer, without any loss in impact strength. The improvement in composites’ mechanical properties comes from well-dispersed nanofibers, increased interfacial interaction, and higher polymer matrix crystallinity. This research shows the potential of extrusion fibrillation for recycling old corrugated containers as a reinforcing material in PLA composites.
W7222752631.title: Pulp Fiber-Reinforced Polylactic Acid (PLA) Nanocomposites Prepared by In Situ Extrusion Fibrillation

W7222761474.abstract: The Tumbler is an open-top flame-cap kiln for making biochar. Its frame is a pear-shaped hexagonal prism, the shape commonly called a hopper. Each end is a hexagon with a flat bottom edge, two lower facets at 35° and two upper facets at 70° from horizontal. The kiln rests upright on its flat bottom and can be rolled onto a facet to load, tend and dump the charge; frame members act as the stops. The kiln has no hood, no cover and no moving parts. The sheet-metal walls hang from the frame and carry no load. This disclosure gives the idealized geometry, a member list for a welded frame, and a bend-and-bolt version built from 3/4" EMT conduit with no welding, plus dimensions, materials, a cut list and variations. It is published to place the design in the public record and to make it free for anyone to build, use and change, under CC BY-SA 4.0.

W7222790941.abstract: Antibiotic accumulation in discharged water is a growing global public health concern that demands high-performance membrane materials to mitigate it. Herein, functionalized zwitterionic biochar (ZBC) was incorporated into a novel membrane composite of polyethersulfone/sulfonated poly(arylene ether sulfone) (PES/SPAES) via the phase-inversion process. Several instrumental characterizations confirmed the fabrication of the composite membrane and the incorporation of the nanofiller into its matrix. ZBC integration altered the membrane morphology, pore structure, hydrophilicity, and surface charge, as well as the thermal and mechanical properties. The best-performing composite membrane achieved an outstanding 99.1% tetracycline (TC) removal efficiency at a permeation flux of 64.1 L m −2 h −1 . The membrane maintained its high performance across complex environments, including mixed-antibiotic solutions (98.5%) and antibiotic-loaded real municipal wastewater (94.8%). The membrane exhibited strong antifouling behavior, long-term operation, and high rejection of natural organic matter (NOM). Feed pH variation confirmed its effect on TC separation, achieving superior TC removal under acidic and alkaline conditions (99.9%), with an enhanced flux of 71.8 L m −2 h −1 at pH 3. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations supported the experimental findings, showing enhanced TC–membrane interaction in the PES/SPAES/ZBC system through reduced energy gap, increased electron-transfer capacity, and stable TC-bound configurations. These findings establish ZBC nanofiller and PES/SPAES composite as promising materials for developing high-performance composite membranes for antibiotic removal.
W7222790941.title: Hybrid zwitterionic biochar-PES-SPAES composite membranes for efficient treatment of antibiotic-laden municipal wastewater

W7222798443.abstract: ABSTRACT Developing high‐performance and magnetically recoverable photocatalysts through rational structural engineering is an effective strategy for improving the photocatalytic degradation of antibiotic pollutants. In this work, a Bimodified ZnFe 2 O 4 /biochar composite (BBZ) was successfully synthesized via a facile hydrothermal method by combining magnetic ZnFe 2 O 4 nanoparticles with biomassderived biochar. The optimized 0.09BBZ delivered the best adsorptionphotocatalytic performance for tetracycline (TC), with 87.3% removal within 180 min under visible light, 74.9% and 10.1% higher than pristine biochar and ZnFe 2 O 4 /biochar (BZ), respectively. Characterizations confirmed Bidoping and biochar synergistically improved physicochemical properties via widened visible‐light absorption, narrowed bandgap, accelerated interfacial charge transfer and inhibited electronhole recombination, boosting photocatalytic activity. Moreover, BBZ possessed favorable magnetic recyclability and stability, retaining 75% TC removal after five cycles. This work demonstrates that the combined strategy of elemental modification and biochar coupling provides an effective route for regulating the electronic structure and photocatalytic properties of ZnFe 2 O 4 ‐based materials, offering a promising photocatalyst for the efficient removal of antibiotic contaminants from water.
W7222798443.title: Electronic Structure Regulation of Bi‐Modified ZnFe 2 O 4 /Biochar for Efficient Tetracycline Photodegradation

W7222801497.abstract: Bio-based and biodegradable plastics are increasingly considered sustainable alternatives to fossil-based plastics due to their potential for environmental benefits and circularity. However, evaluating their overall sustainability requires assessment of environmental impacts across the entire life cycle to avoid burden shifting and unintended consequences. This study presents a critical review and gap analysis of 63 published life cycle assessments (LCA) studies on bio-based compostable plastics, focusing particularly on compostable plastic and how end-of-life is modelled. The review identifies key data gaps and methodological limitations that affect the accuracy of environmental evaluations. Key findings reveal the inconsistent modelling approaches for composting processes, with significant data gaps concerning the temporal dynamics of CO₂ emissions during biodegradation, the environmental consequences of compost application to soil, and polymer-specific degradation rates that determine the persistence of materials and their potential contribution to plastic leakage. The analysis highlights the need for material-specific life cycle inventory (LCI) data capturing emissions to air and impacts on soil, as well as improved reporting of plastic leakage and microplastic flows, for which inventory methods and characterization factors are increasingly available but remain unevenly applied. Addressing these gaps is essential for improving the reliability and completeness of environmental assessments of compostable plastics.
W7222801497.title: Life cycle assessment of compostable plastics: critical review and gap analysis

W7222802140.abstract: Rice is the staple food for over half of the global population and faces escalating threats from climate change, soil degradation, and nutrient leaching that undermine long-term production sustainability. Biochar, a carbon-rich product of biomass pyrolysis under oxygen-limited conditions, has emerged as a promising soil amendment for rice ecosystems, improving soil physicochemical properties including porosity, pH, water retention, and nutrient availability and fostering diverse microbial communities that drive nutrient cycling and soil fertility. By enhancing the abundance and activity of nitrogen-fixing bacteria, mycorrhizal fungi, and phosphorus-solubilizing microorganisms, biochar strengthens the biological foundation of rice productivity, supporting improvements in root development, biomass accumulation, and grain yield. Across the reviewed literature, biochar application has been associated with yield increases generally ranging from approximately 8 to 24% at biochar dosage of 5 to 20 t/ha and nitrogen use efficiency improvements of around 10–12%, though these outcomes are highly dependent on biochar feedstock, pyrolysis conditions, application rate, soil type, and rice genotype. Biochar has also demonstrated capacity to reduce nutrient leaching, mitigate drought and salinity stress, and enhance plant resistance to biotic stressors through rhizosphere microbial modifications. Environmentally, biochar contributes to carbon sequestration and has been associated with reductions in methane and nitrous oxide emissions in paddy systems under specific management conditions, though some studies report increased methane emissions, particularly in high organic carbon soils at elevated application rates. Water retention, runoff reduction, and irrigation efficiency improvements represent additional conservation benefits, especially in sandy or degraded paddy soils. However, biochar application is not without risks: negative effects on soil microbial communities, nutrient immobilization in certain soil types, ecotoxicological concerns from poorly produced biochars, and high production costs of $51–386 per tonne present significant barriers to widespread adoption. Realizing biochar’s potential in sustainable rice production requires optimized, site-specific application strategies, cost-effective production technologies, and transdisciplinary collaboration among researchers, farmers, and policymakers. W7222811873.abstract: Soil microbial biomass represents the living engine of the soil nutrient cycling system, and its restoration in degraded agricultural soils is a prerequisite for sustainable productivity in Pakistan's intensively managed irrigated plains.The present greenhouse Completely Randomised Design (CRD) study, evaluated five amendment treatments -unamended control, NPK chemical fertilizer, farmyard manure (FYM, 10 t ha⁻¹), biochar (2% w/w), and FYM+biochar combination -for their effects on twelve soil biological, chemical, and crop performance parameters in a severely degraded sandy loam soil (initial MBC 84.4 mg kg⁻¹, SOM 0.42%, pH 8.02).Parameters assessed included microbial biomass carbon (MBC), microbial biomass nitrogen (MBN), basal soil respiration, metabolic quotient (qCO₂), MBC:MBN ratio, soil organic matter (SOM), available nitrogen (N), available phosphorus (P), dehydrogenase activity, urease activity, soil pH, and wheat crop yield.The FYM+biochar combination produced the highest values for all biological and yield parameters: MBC 212.4 mg kg⁻¹ (+151.6%over control), MBN 28.6 mg kg⁻¹ (+130.6%),basal respiration 22.4 mg CO₂ 100 g⁻¹ d⁻¹ (+166.7%),dehydrogenase activity 38.4 µg TPF g⁻¹ 24h⁻¹ (+209.7%),urease activity 62.4 µg NH₄⁺-N g⁻¹ h⁻¹ (+153.7%),and crop yield 5.24 g pot⁻¹ (+84.5% over unamended control).Principal component analysis (PCA) explained 77.2% of total variance across PC1 (52.4%) and PC2 (24.8%), with the FYM+biochar treatment positioned at the extreme positive end of PC1 along with all biological health variables.The metabolic quotient (qCO₂) was lowest under FYM+biochar (0.106), indicating the most efficient microbial community metabolism and the least stressed microbial biomass.These results confirm that FYM combined with biochar is the superior amendment strategy for restoring soil microbial fertility, enzymatic activity, and crop productivity in degraded irrigated soils of Punjab, Pakistan, and provide a mechanistic understanding of the complementary contributions of labile organic substrate (FYM) and structured microhabitat (biochar) to soil biological recovery.
W7222811873.title: Evaluation of Soil Microbial Biomass Carbon, Nitrogen, and Enzymatic Activity in Degraded Soils Amended With Organic and Inorganic Fertilizers

W7222817451.abstract: Abstract This study investigated the effect of niobium (Nb) surface modification of biochar via magnetron sputtering on the adsorption of ivermectin and diclofenac potassium, using an integrated approach combining equilibrium experiments and statistical physics-based adsorption models. The biochar was obtained by pyrolysis and then coated with Nb for 30 min at 150 W DC power. We analyzed adsorption equilibrium data using advanced isotherm models to evaluate the process’s steric and energetic parameters. The results indicated predominantly physisorption, with adsorption energies of 17–19 kJ mol − 1 for ivermectin and approximately 11 kJ mol − 1 for diclofenac. Steric parameters exceeded 1 for both drugs, suggesting multi-molecular adsorption, while modeling indicated the formation of two layers on the material’s surface. For ivermectin, maximum adsorption capacities ranged from 81 to 111 mg g − 1 . Furthermore, increasing temperature enhanced ivermectin’s affinity for the modified biochar, whereas diclofenac showed the opposite behavior, highlighting distinct adsorption responses between the two contaminants. Based on the modeling parameters and the adsorbent’s physicochemical characteristics, the results suggest that ivermectin adsorption may involve dipole–dipole interactions, hydrogen bonding, and π–π interactions, while diclofenac adsorption may involve electrostatic interactions, hydrogen bonding, and π–π interactions. These results show that Nb surface modification distinctly influences the adsorption behavior of the two drugs and highlight the potential of magnetron sputtering as a surface-engineering strategy for developing biochars with differential affinity for pharmaceutical contaminants.

W7222821957.abstract: Abstract This research investigates sewage sludge pyrolysis as a route for biochar production, comparing in natura and pelletized feedstocks under slow pyrolysis conditions. Experiments were conducted in a batch reactor at 400–500 °C, with a heating rate of 5 °C min–1 and a residence time of 60 min under an inert atmosphere. Product yields, including biochar, bio-oil, and noncondensable gases, were systematically quantified. Product yields and physicochemical properties, including elemental composition, BET surface area, and inorganic composition by X-ray fluorescence (XRF), were determined, supported by SEM/EDS analysis. Pelletization significantly enhanced biochar yield under all operating conditions, increasing the average yield from 52.1% for in natura sludge to 75.1% for pellets, with a maximum of 78.9% at 450 °C. From an operational perspective, 400 °C was identified as the optimal condition, achieving a high biochar yield (77.2%) while requiring a relatively low electrical energy consumption of 1.1 kWh. Under this condition, a mass balance efficiency of approximately 95% was achieved, indicating that most of the initial biomass mass was accounted for among the recovered pyrolysis products. SEM analysis revealed that pelletization promotes a more compact precursor structure, which is preserved after pyrolysis, resulting in denser and more homogeneous biochar. EDS results confirmed the retention of mineral phases typical of sewage sludge, with compositional variations depending on feedstock form. Direct Arrhenius kinetic analysis indicated that, among the evaluated reaction-order models, the fourth-order approximation provided the best fit within the active pyrolysis region. Overall, feedstock densification prior to pyrolysis improves solid yield and enhances the balance between biochar production and energy demand. These findings demonstrate that sludge pelletization is a promising strategy for improving the efficiency and viability of thermochemical conversion processes.
authors: Camila Maria Aguiar da Costa Alves
W7222821957.title: Interplay between Densification and Thermochemical Conversion in Sewage Sludge Pyrolysis

W7222823341.abstract: Abstract This bibliometric and critical review examines the evolution of scientific research on biochar application in energy-crop systems, emphasizing biomass productivity, soil quality, and soil carbon sequestration from 2007 to 2025. The bibliometric assessment comprised 409 records retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection and integrated publication trends, thematic evolution, scientific collaboration networks, and agronomic and environmental evidence. Scientific production increased markedly during the period, despite interannual variability, accompanied by a shift from biochar production and physicochemical characterization toward field-scale agronomic performance, soil–biochar interactions, pyrogenic carbon persistence, life-cycle assessment, greenhouse gas mitigation, and engineered biochars. Physicochemical characterization nevertheless remained essential for interpreting biochar functionality. Field evidence indicates that crop responses depend on feedstock origin, pyrolysis conditions, biochar properties, application rate, soil characteristics, crop species, and experimental duration. Long-term studies and assessments of pyrogenic carbon stability support the potential of biochar to increase soil carbon stocks and contribute to durable carbon sequestration, although the magnitude and permanence of these effects vary across pedoclimatic conditions and management systems. Major research gaps include limited standardization of biochar characterization, insufficient long-term field validation under tropical conditions, incomplete evaluation of the environmental safety of modified biochars, and the absence of harmonized indicators integrating biomass productivity, soil carbon dynamics, greenhouse gas emissions, and carbon permanence. Overall, current evidence supports biochar as a soil amendment and carbon-management strategy for low-carbon bioenergy systems when material properties and application practices are aligned with site-specific agronomic constraints and validated under representative field conditions.
W7222823341.title: Biochar for Low-Carbon Energy Crop Systems: Bibliometric Trends, Agronomic Evidence, and Soil Carbon Sequestration Pathways from 2007 to 2025

W7222827048.abstract: ABSTRACT This study presents a novel material design approach for wear‐resistant sandwich‐structured hybrid composites fabricated using dual‐nozzle fused deposition modeling (FDM). By co‐printing commercially available mono‐filaments, this approach prevents the compounding difficulties and enables the strategic placement of nanoparticles and micro‐fibers layers. Two hybrid architectures were produced by combining a nano‐copper polylactic acid (nano‐Cu PLA) phase with either a carbon flake (CF PLA) or short carbon fiber (SCF PLA) reinforced phase. The additive manufacturing process was optimized for flexural performance, followed by systematic tribological evaluation using pin‐on‐disc dry sliding tests under different normal pressures and sliding velocities. Micro‐Computed Tomography revealed an interconnected carbon‐filler network with a dispersed nanoparticle phase and a transition band that enhances mechanical interlocking. The hybrid composite filled with copper nanoparticles and SCF achieved a flexural strength of 97.30 MPa, outperforming its base components. At a contact pressure of 1 MPa and a sliding velocity of 0.2 m/s, the specific wear rate decreased to 3.4 × 10 −7 mm 3 /Nm. Microscopic analysis suggests that copper nanoparticles released at the interface act as rolling agents for exposed fiber tips, and change the contact mode, leading to synergistic wear reduction. These findings provide insights for designing high‐performance tribological components via additive manufacturing.
W7222827048.title: Tribological Behavior of Additively Manufactured Dual‐Material Polymer Composites

W7222829074.abstract: Although biodegradable mulch films (BDMs) are promoted as sustainable alternatives to polyethylene films, their degradation may generate microplastics (MPs) and release chemical additives. In this study, commercial poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate)-based BDM (PBAT-BDM) residues were evaluated as a polymer additive system in a two-year carry-over greenhouse maize experiment. PBAT-BDM fragments were incorporated into soil at 0%, 0.1%, 0.5%, and 1% (w/w), and maize was grown for two consecutive cycles (P 1 and P 2 ) in the same continuously irrigated, residue-amended soil. During degradation, PBAT-BDMs developed progressive surface cracking, increased hydrophilicity, decreased C/O ratios, and generated more PBAT-derived MPs. Ultraviolet absorbers (e.g., UV-234 and UV-360) and organophosphate esters (e.g., AO168=O and TNPP) were also released and showed compound-specific dissipation and organ-dependent accumulation in maize. Increasing PBAT-BDM amendment levels altered soil physicochemical properties, reduced chlorophyll content, and increased antioxidant enzyme activities, particularly in P 2 , indicating carry-over physiological stress after prolonged exposure. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed shifts in the microbial community composition, including changes in the relative abundances of Pseudomonadota , Bacteroidota , Bacillota , and Actinomycetota . Structural equation modeling suggested that additive uptake disrupted antioxidant defense and contributed to maize biomass reduction. These findings indicate that commercial PBAT-BDM residues should be assessed as integrated sources of MPs and additives, rather than as biodegradable polymer matrices alone. They provide a scientific basis for managing the combined pollution risks of biodegradable plastics and their additives in agricultural environments.
W7222829074.title: Carry-over release of microplastics and additives from PBAT mulch film residues affects soil-maize-microbiota system

W7222830064.title: Synergistic effects of biochar and organic fertilizer on the regulation of microbial carbon and nitrogen metabolism in paddy soil to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions

W7222832003.abstract: Abstract Municipal sewage sludge (MSS) from small wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) is difficult to manage because decentralized facilities often lack economically viable treatment options. This study evaluated biochar produced by slow pyrolysis of MSS from a small WWTP (< 10,000 population equivalent) treating exclusively domestic wastewater. Pyrolysis at 400 and 600 °C progressively increased carbonization and structural stability, as indicated by a decrease in the H/C org ratio from 1.84 to 0.31, an increase in the thermostable fraction from 14% to 79%, and an increase in the recalcitrance index from 0.41 to 0.56. Carbon sequestration estimates were method-dependent: the R 50 -based carbon sequestration potential (CS R50 ) was higher for B400 (17.5%) than for B600 (15.3%), whereas the H/C org -based 100-year permanence approach predicted greater long-term carbon retention for B600 (0.12 vs. 0.10 kg C/kg dry MSS). These estimates should therefore be regarded as method-dependent predictions. Although total heavy metal concentrations increased during pyrolysis, their mobility decreased markedly, reducing the ecological risk index from 940 to 20. Among priority PAHs, only phenanthrene was detected in B600 at 0.011 mg/kg. Pyrolysis also strongly reduced the phytotoxicity of raw MSS. Overall, slow pyrolysis improved carbon stability and environmental performance. These findings indicate that pyrolysis can provide a locally applicable sludge valorization route for small decentralized WWTPs, combining waste reduction with carbon stabilization and reduced environmental risk.

W7222847294.abstract: To address the limited adsorption capacity, poor pH adaptability, and lack of resource utilization pathways after saturation of conventional adsorbents in the treatment of low-concentration phosphorus-containing wastewater, an LDH@BC composite was synthesized by loading Mg Al layered double hydroxide (LDH) onto sawdust biochar via a ‘physical mixing-carbonization composite’ strategy. Batch experiments showed that at an adsorbent dosage of 0.32 g/L, LDH@BC achieved a maximum phosphate adsorption capacity of 160.59 mg/g, which was 13.3 times that of pristine biochar, and maintained removal efficiencies of 84.7%–95.5% over pH 3–11. In fixed-bed tests, 1 g of LDH@BC maintained >91% phosphate removal from a 1.0 mg/L influent, effectively treating 4440 mL, with the 0.5 mg/L breakthrough at ~7300 mL. Approximately 137 g of LDH@BC would treat 1 ton of such wastewater, demonstrating promising potential for advanced low-concentration phosphate treatment. The adsorption kinetics followed the pseudo-second-order model (R 2 > 0.97), and the isotherm fitted the Freundlich model (R 2 = 0.963), indicating heterogeneous multilayer adsorption dominated by chemisorption. Mechanistic analysis indicated that the synergistic effect of ion exchange and ligand exchange was the dominant mechanism for the efficient adsorption, in which the metal sites on the LDH layers played a key role. In addition, phosphate-saturated LDH@BC was applied in soil pot experiments and promoted the growth of marigold, preliminarily verifying its resource recovery potential as a slow-release phosphorus source. This study provides a material design strategy and an engineering-viable solution for the advanced treatment of low-concentration phosphorus-containing wastewater and phosphorus resource recycling.

W7222892980.abstract: This study reports the development of fully bio-based polylactic acid (PLA) biocomposites reinforced with short Ampelodesmos mauritanicus (Diss) fibers using a powder-based processing route. To improve fiber-matrix compatibility, the fibers were subjected to sequential HCl/NaOH treatment to modify their surface morphology. A fixed concentration of 10 wt.% was selected to isolate the effect of surface treatment on fiber-matrix interaction rather than to optimize the reinforcement level. Multiscale characterization using SEM, AFM, FTIR, Raman spectroscopy, and DSC showed that the treatment improved interfacial adhesion by promoting mechanical interlocking and molecular interactions between PLA and the exposed cellulose-rich fiber surface. AFM observations confirmed a marked increase in surface roughness, while DSC analysis revealed that treated fibers influenced PLA crystallization through the combined effects of heterogeneous nucleation and restricted chain mobility at the interface. These microstructural changes enhanced load transfer, with the treated-fiber composite reaching a Young’s modulus of 4.24 GPa and a tensile strength of 46.8 MPa. The powder-processing route also promoted homogeneous fiber dispersion and may help reduce thermal and shear-induced degradation compared with conventional melt processing. Overall, the results demonstrate that combining interfacial engineering with powder processing provides an effective strategy for designing lightweight, high-performance, and sustainable PLA/Diss biocomposites.
W7222892980.title: Interfacial engineering, processing, and microstructure relationships in PLA/Diss fiber biocomposites for improved mechanical performance

W7222899462.abstract: Polyhydroxyalkanoates are a family of biopolymers that accumulate inside microorganisms as primary storage polymers in response to nutrient stress. This family of biopolymers can be used as bioplastics instead of synthetic plastics because it biodegrades into CO2 and H2O. This study aimed to isolate a new bacterial strain that can accumulate PHAs when cultured under unbalanced nutrient conditions of excess carbon and a depleted nitrogen source. Screening for PHAs accumulating bacterial isolates was based on culturing the bacteria on minimal salt medium containing Nile red as a fluorescent dye. Positive PHAs bacterial colonies displayed bright orange fluorescence under ultraviolet light while PHA- negative isolates failed to exhibit fluorescence. Extraction of PHAs was achieved using a dispersion of sodium hypochlorite-chloroform solution and quantified by conversion into crotonic acid through boiling in concentrated sulfuric acid and measured by UV spectrophotometer at 235 nm. The most potent isolate was selected to optimize cell growth and PHAs production conditions using the ``one- factor-at-a-time'' method. The newly isolated strain Corynebacterium variabile M11 was identified using the 16S rRNA gene and characterized as a positive PHAs-accumulating bacterium using staining and fluorescent tests. Granules were observed inside the cytoplasm by (TEM). The structure of extracted PHAs was analyzed by FTIR and 1H-NMR spectroscopy, and the results confirmed the similarity with standard PHAs and were characterized as poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3- hydroxyvalerate). The optimum pH, temperature, and incubation period for maximum PHA production using dextrose and ammonium chloride were 7, 30 °C, and 72 h, respectively.
W7222899462.title: Production and Optimization of Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) by Corynebacterium Variabile M11: A Newly Reported PHAs-Producing Bacterium
